$comment: Rule catalog — health. Contains exactly the thirteen health prohibitions from the source specification, plus eight rules about what an interpretation must record. The prohibition count is pinned in artifacts/rule-inventory.json and checked by scripts/rules.mjs; each prohibition's description reproduces the source's own line verbatim and is checked by scripts/fidelity.mjs. Between them, a prohibition cannot be removed, downgraded, or reworded without a visible edit to a reviewed file.

rules.title: A condition is never diagnosed solely from one consumer measurement
rules.description: Never diagnose a condition solely from one consumer measurement
rules.rationale: A consumer device measures one quantity under uncontrolled conditions, and a diagnosis is a claim about a person that changes how they act, what they fear, and whether they seek care. A single reading cannot separate the condition from the hundred ordinary things that move the same number, and naming a condition on that basis produces a conclusion the reader cannot easily undo — including one who then stops looking for the real explanation.
rules.remediation: Describe what the measurement shows and what could account for it, including the ordinary explanations. Where a condition is genuinely worth ruling in or out, that is a reason to suggest evaluation by someone qualified to do it, not a reason to name it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment. No mechanical check can establish that a project never draws a diagnostic conclusion from one reading; it reports not-evaluated unless a human review is recorded.

rules.title: A single reading is never treated as a long-term trend
rules.description: Never treat a single reading as a long-term trend
rules.rationale: One point is not a direction. Presenting it as one manufactures a pattern out of noise, and the reader acts on a movement that may reverse tomorrow for reasons nobody recorded.
rules.remediation: Say how many observations the statement rests on and over what period. Where there is only one, say what it is: a single reading.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Measurement quality is never ignored
rules.description: Never ignore measurement quality
rules.rationale: How a measurement was taken determines what it can support. A blood pressure taken after climbing stairs, a sleep stage inferred from wrist movement, a weight taken at a different time of day — each carries an error that can exceed the effect being discussed. Interpreting the number without its quality treats an artifact as a finding.
rules.remediation: Record how the measurement was taken and what that implies about its reliability, then interpret within that limit rather than past it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment. The related requirement health.measurement-quality-recorded checks only that a section exists — never that the assessment in it is right.

rules.title: Medical facts are never fabricated
rules.description: Never fabricate medical facts
rules.rationale: A confident, false medical claim is more dangerous than an admission of ignorance, because it is acted upon. Fabrication includes inventing a reference range, a mechanism, a statistic, or a study — anything asserted with more authority than its actual source supports.
rules.remediation: State what is known, what is uncertain, and what is not known. 'I do not know' is a legitimate and often correct answer.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Health measurements are never fabricated
rules.description: Never fabricate health measurements
rules.rationale: A measurement that was never taken corrupts everything downstream of it, and unlike a wrong interpretation it leaves no trace of being wrong. Estimating a missing value and presenting it as observed is fabrication regardless of how reasonable the estimate was.
rules.remediation: Record measurements as observed, estimated, or unknown, and never move a value between those categories to fill a gap.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: No false reassurance when serious warning signs are present
rules.description: Never provide false reassurance when serious warning signs are present
rules.rationale: This is the failure with the worst consequence in the whole catalog. Reassurance is what a worried person is looking for, so it is readily accepted and rarely questioned — and when it is wrong, it delays care at exactly the moment delay matters most.
rules.remediation: Where warning signs are present, say so plainly and say what to do about them. Reassurance that has to be qualified is not reassurance; give the qualification instead.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment, and the rule where the gap between what a machine can check and what matters is widest. Reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Ordinary measurements are never catastrophized without supporting evidence
rules.description: Never catastrophize ordinary measurements without supporting evidence
rules.rationale: The mirror of false reassurance, and it is not the safe direction. Alarming someone about ordinary variation produces anxiety, unnecessary testing, and — worst — a learned habit of discounting the system, which then applies to the warning that was real.
rules.remediation: Match the concern to the evidence. Where a measurement is within ordinary variation for this person, say that, and say what would change the assessment.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Certainty is never claimed where multiple explanations are possible
rules.description: Never claim certainty where multiple explanations are possible
rules.rationale: Most consumer health observations have several plausible explanations, and the confident presentation of one closes off the others in the reader's mind. Stated certainty is also what makes a wrong conclusion hard to revisit later.
rules.remediation: Name the plausible explanations and what would distinguish them. Confidence should track the evidence, and saying so costs nothing.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: No one is told to ignore serious symptoms
rules.description: Never tell someone to ignore serious symptoms
rules.rationale: Telling someone to disregard a symptom substitutes a judgement the system is not in a position to make, and does so in the direction that forecloses action. Even where the symptom probably is benign, 'probably' is not a basis for instructing someone to stop paying attention.
rules.remediation: Describe what the symptom may indicate and what would warrant evaluation. Where something is likely benign, say that while leaving the reader able to act on it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Wearable measurements are never treated as perfectly accurate
rules.description: Never treat wearable measurements as perfectly accurate
rules.rationale: A wearable displays a number to the same precision whether it measured well or badly, and the display carries no error bar. Sleep staging, blood oxygen, stress scores, and calorie estimates in particular are inferences from proxies, and treating them as ground truth attributes an authority to the device that the device does not claim for itself.
rules.remediation: Treat wearable output as an estimate with a known direction and size of error where that is documented, and say so when it is not.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Causation is never inferred solely from correlation in personal health data
rules.description: Never infer causation solely from correlation in personal health data
rules.rationale: Personal health data is a small sample of an uncontrolled experiment with dozens of moving variables, and it produces coincidences abundantly. A causal claim drawn from it tells someone to change a behavior that may have nothing to do with the outcome, and the change then appears to work for reasons of regression alone.
rules.remediation: Report the association as an association, name what else could produce it, and say what would be needed to establish a cause.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Medications and contextual factors known to materially affect interpretation are never silently ignored
rules.description: Never silently ignore medications or contextual factors known to materially affect interpretation
rules.rationale: A beta blocker changes what a heart rate means; an illness, a time zone, a night shift, a new training block, or a medication started last week each change what a measurement can be compared against. Interpreting without a known modifier is not merely incomplete — it produces a confident answer to a question that was never the one being asked. The word that carries the weight is 'silently': the system may lack the information, but it must not have it and pass over it.
rules.remediation: Record the known medications and contextual factors and state how they bear on the interpretation. Where they are unknown, say that rather than assuming their absence.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment. The related recommendation health.modifiers-recorded checks only that a section exists and is non-empty.

rules.title: Population averages are never substituted for a known individual baseline without acknowledging the difference
rules.description: Never substitute generalized population averages for known individual baseline without acknowledging the difference
rules.rationale: A resting heart rate of 48 is alarming against a population average and unremarkable for the person who has lived at 48 for a decade. Where an individual baseline is known, comparing against the population instead produces a finding about the population, presented as a finding about the person.
rules.remediation: Compare against the individual baseline where one is known. Where only population data is available, say which is being used and what that costs the interpretation.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment; reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.

rules.title: Health interpretations are recorded as durable artifacts
rules.description: An interpretation of a person's health data is written down as a durable record rather than produced and discarded, so that what was concluded, on what evidence, and with what uncertainty can be re-examined later.
rules.rationale: An interpretation nobody kept cannot be revisited when the next measurement arrives, cannot be checked against what actually happened, and cannot be corrected. Durability is also what makes the rest of this catalog checkable at all: a record is the thing evidence attaches to.
rules.remediation: Write interpretations into artifacts/interpretations/ using the interpretation-record template.
rules.$assuranceNote: A detector establishes that interpretation records EXIST. It establishes nothing about whether they are accurate, complete, or sound.

rules.title: Interpretation records include a symptom and context section
rules.description: An interpretation record states the symptoms and circumstances surrounding the measurement — what the person was experiencing, and what was happening around it.
rules.rationale: A number without its circumstances is close to uninterpretable. The same resting heart rate means different things during an illness, after a poor night, in a heat wave, or in the week of a new training block, and the circumstances are usually known at the time and lost afterwards.
rules.remediation: Add a Context section to the record describing symptoms and circumstances, or stating that none were reported.
rules.$assuranceNote: A detector establishes that the section is present and non-empty — never that the context recorded in it is complete or relevant.

rules.title: Interpretation records state measurement quality
rules.description: An interpretation record states how the measurement was taken and what that implies about its reliability — the device, the conditions, and any reason to trust it less than usual.
rules.rationale: Measurement quality is the first thing forgotten and the first thing needed when an interpretation is revisited. Recording it at the time is cheap; reconstructing it later is guesswork.
rules.remediation: Add a Measurement Quality section naming the device, the conditions, and known limitations.
rules.$assuranceNote: A detector establishes that the section is present and non-empty. Whether the quality assessment is correct is health.no-ignored-measurement-quality, which no machine evaluates.

rules.title: Interpretation records reference the individual baseline, or state that none is known
rules.description: An interpretation record names the individual baseline the measurement is being read against, or states explicitly that no individual baseline is known and what is being used instead.
rules.rationale: The alternative to naming the baseline is not neutrality — it is an unstated population comparison. Requiring the record to say which one is in use is what makes the substitution visible when it happens.
rules.remediation: Add a Baseline section naming the individual baseline and its basis, or stating that none is known and what is being used in its place.
rules.$assuranceNote: A detector establishes that the section is present and non-empty — never that the baseline is well founded or that it was actually used in the reasoning.

rules.title: Interpretation records state uncertainty and alternative explanations
rules.description: An interpretation record states how confident the interpretation is and what else could account for the observation.
rules.rationale: Uncertainty recorded at the time is honest; uncertainty added later looks like a retraction. Writing the alternatives down also improves the interpretation, because listing them is what reveals when the leading explanation is not clearly ahead.
rules.remediation: Add an Uncertainty section stating confidence and naming the alternative explanations considered.
rules.$assuranceNote: A detector establishes that the section is present and non-empty. Whether the confidence is calibrated is health.no-unwarranted-certainty, which no machine evaluates.

rules.title: Interpretation records assign one of the four escalation tiers
rules.description: An interpretation record assigns exactly one of the four escalation tiers — normal variation, worth monitoring, worth discussing with a professional, or potentially urgent — so that what the reader should do about it is explicit rather than inferred from tone.
rules.rationale: Without an explicit tier the reader infers urgency from wording, which is the least reliable channel available and the one most affected by whoever wrote it. An explicit tier is also what makes escalation decisions reviewable after the fact.
rules.remediation: Add an Escalation Tier section naming exactly one of the four tiers.
rules.$assuranceNote: A detector establishes that exactly one canonical tier label is present. It establishes nothing about whether it is the RIGHT tier, which is the question that matters and which only a human can answer.

rules.title: Interpretation records note medications and contextual factors, or state that none are known
rules.description: An interpretation record notes medications and other contextual factors that could materially affect the interpretation, or states that none are known.
rules.rationale: A record that is silent about medications is ambiguous between 'none' and 'nobody asked', and only one of those supports an interpretation. This is a recommendation rather than a requirement because many legitimate projects never hold medication data at all; where it is held, the prohibition on silently ignoring it applies with full force.
rules.remediation: Add a Medications and Contextual Factors section, stating explicitly when none are known.
rules.$assuranceNote: A detector establishes that the section is present and non-empty. Whether a known modifier was actually taken into account is health.no-silently-ignored-modifiers, which no machine evaluates.

rules.title: Guidance labels the strength of the evidence behind its claims
rules.description: Health claims carry an indication of how well established they are, so that a reader can tell a robust finding from a plausible mechanism from a single small study.
rules.rationale: Claims presented at uniform confidence are read at uniform confidence, and the weakest one borrows the credibility of the strongest. Labelling evidence strength is also the practical defence against fabricated facts: a claim that cannot be labelled usually cannot be sourced.
rules.remediation: Indicate the strength of the evidence behind each substantive claim, and say when a claim rests on mechanism or extrapolation rather than direct evidence.
rules.$assuranceNote: Judgment. Reports not-evaluated without a recorded human review.
